claim_text: Nicaea (325) was about the Arian controversy and the Nicene Creed — NOT the canon.

secondary_sources.citation: Henry Chadwick, The Early Church (Penguin, rev. ed. 1993)
Frances Young, From Nicaea to Chalcedon (Baker Academic, 2nd ed. 2010)

counterargument: Popular skeptic accounts claim Constantine assembled the council to select or suppress scriptures. No primary source supports this; the council's agenda was exclusively Christological and disciplinary.
notes: This is the single most commonly encountered popular misconception in this corpus's subject area. Flagged in Method §2 reference table as explicitly false.

claim_text: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) is the first extrabiblical mention of Israel, as a people not a place.

secondary_sources.citation: James K. Hoffmeier, Israel in Egypt (Oxford University Press, 1997)
Frank J. Yurco, '3,200-Year-Old Picture of Israelites Found in Egypt,' Biblical Archaeology Review 16(5) 1990

notes: The determinative sign on 'Israel' in the stele marks it as a people/ethnic group rather than a territory, which is the basis for the 'people not a place' distinction. This is the scholarly consensus reading.

claim_text: Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem (701 BCE) is the best-corroborated event in the Hebrew Bible.

secondary_sources.citation: William Hallo and K. Lawson Younger, eds., The Context of Scripture, vol. 2 (Brill, 2000)

counterargument: 'Best-corroborated' is a comparative claim. The Assyrian and biblical accounts diverge on outcome — Sennacherib claims tribute and withdrawal; the Bible records an angel destroying the army. The event's occurrence is corroborated; its outcome is contested between sources.
notes: Qualification added: corroboration is for the event, not the outcome. The 'best-corroborated' framing is defensible but should include this distinction in the public text.

claim_text: Paul's undisputed letters (c. 50–60 CE) are the earliest Christian writings that survive and contain no birth narrative, no empty tomb, no biography.

primary_sources.source: 1 Thessalonians, Galatians, 1–2 Corinthians, Romans, Philippians, Philemon
primary_sources.locator: Full texts; see also 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 for the resurrection tradition

secondary_sources.citation: Raymond E. Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament (Doubleday, 1997)

notes: The absence of birth narrative and empty tomb in Paul is a factual observation about Paul's surviving letters, not a theological claim. 1 Cor 15:3–8 does reference resurrection appearances, which should not be conflated with the empty-tomb narratives of the Gospels.

claim_text: The original Sunday labor laws were motivated by religious forces, while the Maryland law's purpose and effect by 1961 had become a secular day of rest and recreation.

secondary_sources.citation: U.S. Supreme Court syllabus and opinion, McGowan v. Maryland, 366 U.S. 420 (1961)
secondary_sources.locator: Historical review and present-purpose analysis, pp. 431–449

counterargument: The religious origin of Sunday-closing laws does not establish that the 1961 Maryland statute had a religious operative purpose. McGowan expressly separated origin from then-current secular rationale.
notes: This claim is used to demonstrate the project's core separation between historical origin and current legal rationale.

claim_text: The Morrill Anti-Bigamy Act was aimed at Utah Mormons and plural marriage, while broader federal territorial and slavery/state-rights politics also shaped the legislative context.

secondary_sources.locator: Discussion of anti-polygamy legislation, territorial regulation, slavery, and states' rights; https://www.archives.gov/publications/prologue/2017/winter/summer-of-1862

counterargument: The sources establish both a direct anti-polygamy/Mormon target and a broader political setting; they do not permit a precise numerical weighting of religious versus territorial or sectional motives.
notes: Category C is used because official sources document both a religion-linked target and substantial nonreligious territorial/sectional context.

claim_text: Indiana's Choice Scholarship Program has a documented secular educational-choice purpose even though religiously affiliated schools may participate.

primary_sources.source: Indiana Department of Education, Choice Scholarship Program
primary_sources.locator: Current program description and statutory authorization under IC 20-51-1 and IC 20-51-4; https://www.in.gov/doe/students/indiana-choice-scholarship-program/
Discussion of direct beneficiaries and valid secular purpose; https://public.courts.in.gov/Decisions/api/Document/Opinion?Id=J05Ps3rV8U8J5E21jpQdtFtZSesxhcvjxGMBDHpC6068_qeh1SUJ_1q8NJaE72_C0

counterargument: A secular program purpose does not establish that religious organizations played no role in school-choice advocacy or that religious schools receive no incidental benefit; Meredith expressly treated such school benefits as ancillary to family educational choice.
notes: Category E concerns documented program purpose, not a claim that every actor supporting the policy had a secular motive.

claim_text: Pew's 2023–24 Religious Landscape Study estimates Indiana adults as 32% evangelical Protestant, 16% Catholic, 11% mainline Protestant, 3% historically Black Protestant, 5% atheist, 4% agnostic, and 21% nothing in particular, with a ±5.0 percentage-point margin of error for adults in Indiana.

primary_sources.source: Pew Research Center, 2023–24 Religious Landscape Study — Indiana
primary_sources.locator: State religious-composition table and state margin-of-error note; https://www.pewresearch.org/religious-landscape-study/state/indiana/

counterargument: These are survey estimates, not census counts. Small differences should not be treated as precise population gaps, and percentages can be affected by rounding and categories reported as less than 1%.
notes: The population context layer is kept separate from legal-causation coding.

claim_text: As of September 27, 2026, 3 of 6 tracked Indiana power positions have publicly documented religious affiliations in the sources reviewed; all three documented affiliations are Christian, while the remaining three are unknown, so the religious composition of the full six-position set cannot be determined.

primary_sources.source: Indiana Governor — official biography of Mike Braun
Indiana Lieutenant Governor — official biography of Micah Beckwith
primary_sources.locator: Biography states more than 15 years as Worship Pastor and Campus Pastor; https://www.in.gov/lg/about-the-office/biography/

primary_sources.source: Indiana Senate Republicans — Rodric Bray biography
primary_sources.locator: Current office and First United Methodist Church of Martinsville listed in activities; https://www.indianasenaterepublicans.com/bray

primary_sources.source: Indiana Attorney General — official biography of Todd Rokita
primary_sources.locator: Current officeholder; no affiliation stated in biography reviewed; https://www.in.gov/attorneygeneral/about-the-office/about-the-attorney-general/

primary_sources.source: Indiana House Republicans — Todd Huston biography
primary_sources.locator: Current Speaker; no affiliation stated in biography reviewed; https://www.indianahouserepublicans.com/members/leadership/todd-huston/

primary_sources.source: Indiana Judicial Branch — Chief Justice Loretta H. Rush biography
primary_sources.locator: Current Chief Justice; no affiliation stated in biography reviewed; https://www.in.gov/courts/supreme/justices/loretta-rush

counterargument: Publicly documented coverage is incomplete. 'Unknown' means no reliable affiliation was identified in the sources reviewed, not that the officeholder is nonreligious. The documented subset therefore cannot establish a religious majority across all six tracked positions.
notes: Tracked set: governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, House speaker, Senate president pro tempore/equivalent, and chief justice.
